newsitem.title: USA: NASA may delay space station construction.
newsitem.headline: NASA may delay space station construction.

text.p: The U.S. space agency may delay construction of its troubled international space station by six months, sources close to the project said on Tuesday.

NASA officials were considering delaying the start of assembly of the $40 billion orbiting laboratory from this November until May 1998 because a key Russian component called the Service Module is running late, according to the sources, who asked not to be identified.

The space agency was also leaning toward purchasing a $98 million Russian space tug, instead of a U.S.-built one, to maintain the station's altitude in case the service module is delayed further, the sources said. The Russian tug, known by the acronym FGB-2, could be ready to fly in June 1998 and would be designed to be refueled by the U.S. shuttle.
Debra Rahn, spokeswoman for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, said space station officials were unavailable for comment but acknowledged that a six-month delay was being considered.
"It is one of the many options we are looking at," she said. "We have made no final decisions."

Despite technical and funding problems, NASA has so far resisted delaying the start of space station construction for fear of losing political support. White House science adviser John Gibbons and NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin were to testify on Wednesday before the House of Representatives Committee on Science on the status of Russia's participation in the space station.

The space agency has struggled recently to accommodate the expected late arrival of the Russian Service Module, which was to serve as a control centre and living quarters during construction of the outpost. It was scheduled for launch in May 1998 but was running up to eight months behind schedule because of a lack of funding from the Russian government.

U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, meeting last weekend, drew up a plan to get Russian government money flowing to the contractors building the Service Module.

"We went over, in intricate detail, exactly what flows of money have to go to which players and which contractors in Russia by which dates," Gore said on Sunday. "And (Chernomyrdin) has got it clearly in his mind ...
"I think that the assurances now are backed up by a practical checklist of which dates and which amounts, and I hope it's going to work," Gore said.

NASA recently began advancing $20 million in payments to the Russian space agency to kick-start construction of the module, Goldin said last week. With full funding from Russia, the Service Module could be rescheduled for launch as early as October 1998, the sources said. That would be followed by the first space station crew in November or December of that year.

The space station has been on the drawing board for more than a decade and was repeatedly delayed by U.S. lawmakers who balked at its multibillion-dollar cost. The project gained political favour when Russia joined the international effort.
